narrative:
Your application to law school has been denied based on a predictive assessment that identified a very high likelihood — 99.2% — that you would not pass the bar exam on your first attempt. This is an incredibly difficult outcome to receive, and it's important that you understand exactly what drove this decision so you can take meaningful steps forward.

The most influential factor in this assessment was your academic performance in your third year of undergraduate study. Your grades placed you in the 2nd decile within your school, meaning roughly 80% of your classmates performed above you during that critical final stretch of your undergraduate education. Among students who have gone on to pass the bar exam, the average third-year standing is closer to the 6th decile — a substantial gap that weighed heavily in this prediction. This pattern was reinforced by your first-year academic standing, which also placed you in the 2nd decile, suggesting that the academic challenges you faced were not a temporary setback but a consistent trend throughout your undergraduate years. Together, these two factors were by far the strongest drivers of the model's concern about your readiness for the rigors of law school and the bar exam.

The third factor that contributed to this outcome, though less influential than your academic record, was your family income background. You come from an upper-middle income household, which is actually the most common background among students who pass the bar — about 45% of successful students share this profile. This means your family background did not work against you in any meaningful way, but it also wasn't enough to offset the academic signals the model identified.

It's also worth noting that your LSAT score of 34 and undergraduate GPA of 2.90 fall below the averages of students who passed the bar (37.27 and 3.24, respectively), and while these were not among the top three factors flagged, they paint a consistent picture alongside your decile rankings. The fact that you plan to attend full-time is a positive circumstance — over 93% of students who pass the bar attend full-time, just as you intend — but it was not enough to shift the overall assessment.

As a next step, you are strongly encouraged to consider investing time in strengthening your academic foundation before reapplying. Pursuing additional coursework, retaking the LSAT to improve your score, or enrolling in a post-baccalaureate program to demonstrate improved academic performance could meaningfully change this outcome. Speaking with an academic advisor or pre-law counselor about a structured plan would be a valuable use of your time, and many students who initially face setbacks like this go on to succeed after targeted preparation.
